lead: A system at fixed temperature has two useful energy buckets: Helmholtz free energy A = U − TS for fixed volume, and Gibbs free energy G = H − TS for fixed pressure. They subtract the unavailable energy TS from internal energy or enthalpy, leaving the part that can become work. Industry uses G for reactors, separators and phase changes at constant pressure; A appears in statistical mechanics and constant-volume calculations. This chapter defines A and G, gives their differentials, equilibrium tests and one worked compression example.
prereq: You need: internal energy and enthalpy from Unit 1, and entropy from Unit 3; the full set of differentials is in 4.2.

blocks.text: A system at temperature T holds internal energy U. Part of U is tied to the random motion counted by entropy S: the product TS. Subtract that part and the remainder is Helmholtz free energy A = U − TS. The same idea at constant pressure starts from enthalpy H = U + PV, so Gibbs free energy G = H − TS = U + PV − TS. Here U is internal energy (J), H is enthalpy (J), T is absolute temperature (K), S is entropy (J/K), P is pressure (Pa), V is volume (m³). A and G carry units of J; per mole they are J/mol.

The subtraction TS removes energy that cannot become work in a reversible isothermal step. A is used when volume is fixed, as in a rigid bomb or a statistical-mechanics lattice. G is used when pressure is fixed, which is the usual laboratory, reactor and pipe condition. Some syllabi call A the Helmholtz free energy F; F and A mean the same property.

For a closed system with only pressure-volume work, dU = T dS − P dV. Differentiate A = U − TS: dA = dU − T dS − S dT. Put dU in: dA = −S dT − P dV. Differentiate G = H − TS with dH = T dS + V dP: dG = −S dT + V dP. These are exact differentials for A(T,V) and G(T,P). The variables in brackets are the natural variables: T and V for A, T and P for G.

blocks.where: A is Helmholtz free energy (J); S entropy (J/K); T absolute temperature (K); P pressure (Pa); V volume (m³).
G is Gibbs free energy (J); the other symbols are defined above.

blocks.text: At constant T and V, the second law gives dA ≤ 0 for a spontaneous change in a closed system with only PV work; dA = 0 at equilibrium. At constant T and P, dG ≤ 0, and dG = 0 at equilibrium. The inequality is the practical test: a process at fixed T and P proceeds only if G falls. Work interpretation: at constant T and V, the maximum work obtainable is −ΔA; at constant T and P, the maximum non-PV useful work obtainable is −ΔG.

blocks.where: This is the Gibbs-Helmholtz equation; G is Gibbs free energy (J), T is temperature (K), H is enthalpy (J).

sections.h3: Signs and the isothermal ideal-gas result

blocks.text: For an isothermal process on an ideal gas, ΔU = 0 and ΔH = 0. Then ΔA = −TΔS and ΔG = −TΔS, so ΔA = ΔG. The entropy change for n moles going from P1 to P2 at constant T is ΔS = nR ln(P1/P2). Therefore ΔA = ΔG = nRT ln(P2/P1). Here n is moles (mol), R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, T is in K, and P1 and P2 are initial and final pressures in the same unit.

Compression has P2 > P1, so ln(P2/P1) > 0 and both ΔA and ΔG are positive. Positive means the surroundings must supply work; the gas does not release it. Expansion gives a negative value. For a real gas or a phase change, ΔA and ΔG differ because ΔU and ΔH are not zero. At constant T,P, a negative ΔG marks a spontaneous phase change or reaction; see Unit 5 for chemical potential.

figure.caption: U is changed to A by subtracting TS and to H by adding PV; H becomes G by subtracting TS. Notice that the direct route from A to G adds PV, so both routes give the same G.

spec.title: From U to A and G
spec.aria: U is transformed to A by subtracting TS and to H by adding PV; H is transformed to G by subtracting TS.

examples.question: One mole of ideal gas at 300 K is compressed isothermally and reversibly from 1 bar to 5 bar. Calculate ΔA and ΔG. Treat the gas as ideal.
steps: For an ideal gas at constant T, ΔU = 0 and ΔH = 0.
The entropy change is ΔS = nR ln(P1/P2) = 1 × 8.314 × ln(1/5) = 8.314 × (−1.6094) = −13.38 J/K.
examples.answer: ΔA = ΔG = +4.01 kJ, so work must be supplied to compress the gas.
examples.check:
import math
n = 1.0
R = 8.314
T = 300.0
P1 = 1.0
P2 = 5.0
dS = n * R * math.log(P1 / P2)
dA = n * R * T * math.log(P2 / P1)
dG = dA
print(round(dA / 1000, 2))
print(round(dG / 1000, 2))

traps: Writing G = U − TS instead of G = H − TS. Check that G = U + PV − TS; the PV term is missing in the wrong form.
Using Celsius in T. Every free-energy formula uses absolute temperature in kelvin.
Losing the sign for compression. If P2 > P1, ln(P2/P1) is positive, so ΔA and ΔG are positive; expansion gives negative values.
Swapping the equilibrium tests. dA ≤ 0 belongs to constant T,V; dG ≤ 0 belongs to constant T,P.
Forgetting that ΔA = ΔG is a special result for an ideal gas at constant T. For a real gas or phase change, ΔA = ΔU − TΔS and ΔG = ΔH − TΔS are different.

quiz.q: Define Helmholtz free energy A and Gibbs free energy G. Give their units.
quiz.a: A = U − TS and G = H − TS = U + PV − TS. Both have units of J, or J/mol per mole.

quiz.q: Why does subtracting TS turn U or H into a useful work function?
quiz.a: TS is the energy tied to entropy at temperature T. Removing it leaves the part of U or H that can be converted to work in a reversible isothermal process.

quiz.q: Two moles of ideal gas at 400 K expand isothermally and reversibly from 10 bar to 2 bar. Find ΔA and ΔG.
At constant T and P a reaction has ΔG = +2 kJ. Is it spontaneous as written? What if ΔG = −2 kJ?
quiz.a: With ΔG = +2 kJ the reaction is not spontaneous as written; the reverse direction is favoured. With ΔG = −2 kJ the forward reaction is spontaneous.

quiz.q: Write dA and dG for a closed simple compressible system.
quiz.a: dA = −S dT − P dV and dG = −S dT + V dP.

quiz.q: What does −ΔG represent at constant T and P?
quiz.a: −ΔG is the maximum non-PV useful work obtainable from the process at constant T and P.

quiz.q: Compare the meaning of dA ≤ 0 at constant T,V with dG ≤ 0 at constant T,P.
quiz.a: At constant T,V, a spontaneous closed-system change lowers A; at equilibrium dA = 0. At constant T,P, a spontaneous change lowers G; at equilibrium dG = 0. The fixed variables decide which free energy is the criterion.

quiz.q: Use the Gibbs-Helmholtz equation to state the sign of ∂(G/T)/∂T at constant P when H is positive.
quiz.a: ∂(G/T)/∂T at constant P = −H/T². If H is positive and T is positive, the derivative is negative.

beyond: Not for the exam. Process simulators use Gibbs free energy to decide phase splits and reaction directions at fixed pressure. Materials science uses Helmholtz free energy for solid-state transformations at fixed volume. Statistical mechanics connects A to the partition function, which links molecular models to bulk properties.
